posts.image_prompt: Archaeologists in 1930s clothing kneeling in a vast sandy trench on an English heath, the ghostly outline of a long wooden ship preserved only as neat rows of rusted iron nails in the sand, a woman in a long coat and hat watching from the edge, soft golden late-summer light, cinematic
posts.caption:
⚓ A SHIP BURIED UNDER AN ENGLISH FIELD

In the late 1930s, landowner Edith Pretty asked a self-taught local excavator named Basil Brown to dig into the mysterious mounds on her estate at Sutton Hoo, in Suffolk, England.

In 1939 he found something nobody expected: the outline of a ship more than 80 feet long. The wood had rotted away completely. Only its 'ghost' remained — rows of iron nails still sitting in the sand.

In the middle was a burial chamber full of treasure: a gold belt buckle, silver tableware from distant lands, and a full-face iron helmet unlike anything ever found in Britain.

But there was no body. Acidic soil may have dissolved it.

Most historians think this was the grave of Rædwald, King of East Anglia, who died around 624 AD. Nobody can prove it.

Edith Pretty donated the entire find to the British Museum.

Would you have given away a king's treasure found in your own garden?

posts.title: The explosion that left no crater

scenes.image_prompt: A blinding bluish fireball streaking across a pale morning sky above an endless Siberian pine forest, early 1900s, dramatic cinematic light
scenes.narration: In 1908, something exploded over Siberia and flattened a forest. It left no crater.

scenes.narration: It happened on the morning of June thirtieth, nineteen-oh-eight, over a remote stretch of forest in Siberia, in the Russian Empire.

posts.caption:
☄️ 80 million trees flattened. No crater. No meteorite.

On June 30, 1908, a blast over remote Siberia levelled around 2,150 square kilometres of forest. Scientists believe an asteroid or comet exploded in mid-air.

Rock or ice — which do you think it was? 👇

posts.image_prompt: A Norse warrior standing on a rocky Scandinavian shore beside a longship, wearing a simple rounded iron helmet with an eye-and-nose guard and no horns, wool tunic and round wooden shield on his back, misty fjord, cinematic natural light
posts.caption:
🪖 VIKINGS NEVER WORE HORNED HELMETS

It's one of history's most famous images — and it's wrong.

The most complete Viking helmet ever found was dug up at Gjermundbu, Norway, in 1943. It dates to the 10th century. It's a rounded iron cap with a guard for the eyes and nose. No horns.

So where did the horns come from? Largely from an opera.

For an 1876 production of Richard Wagner's 'Der Ring des Nibelungen', costume designer Carl Emil Doepler gave the Norse characters horned helmets. The look stuck — in paintings, cartoons and films.

Real fighters had good reason to skip them: horns could snag on branches or catch an enemy's blow.

What other 'fact' about the Vikings do you suspect is a myth?
